body:
How Gujarat was connected with the Roman world

During the early centuries CE, the Roman Empire controlled Egypt. Egypt's Red Sea ports therefore served as important starting points for commercial voyages between the Roman world and the Indian Ocean.

Two prominent Egyptian ports were Myos Hormos and Berenice. Ships could sail from the Red Sea, pass through the waters near Arabia and cross the Arabian Sea toward the western coast of India. Barygaza was one of the important destinations of this trade.

Goods obtained from India could move through Egyptian trading routes toward Mediterranean markets. Conversely, merchants arriving from Roman Egypt and other regions brought foreign goods to Indian ports.

Connections were not limited to Rome

Gujarat also maintained commercial contacts with Arabia, the Persian Gulf and East Africa. The Periplus refers to shipping between Barygaza and markets on the Arabian and East African sides of the Indian Ocean. It records Indian cloth and food products among the goods carried on some of these routes.

Overseas commerce involved merchants and sailors from different regions. Indo-Roman trade refers to commercial connections with the Roman world; it does not imply that every ship or merchant was Roman.

The importance of monsoon winds

The monsoon is a seasonal wind system whose prevailing direction changes during the year. Knowledge of this pattern made long-distance maritime voyages more practical.

  • South-west monsoon: During the summer season, these winds could assist vessels travelling from the Arabian or East African side of the sea toward India's western coast.
  • North-east monsoon: During the cooler part of the year, the prevailing winds could assist the return journey westward.

The Periplus mentions a favourable sailing period around July for ships travelling from Egypt to Barygaza. The actual safety of a voyage still depended on winds, sea conditions and the difficulties of entering particular harbours.

Roman coins and the meaning of commercial contact

Roman coins found in India, especially in southern India, provide evidence of commercial contact between Indian markets and the Roman world. Coins could enter trade as payments or valuable metal and could circulate beyond their original place of issue.

However, the discovery of Roman coins does not prove Roman political control over the region where they are found. Indian kingdoms and merchant communities could trade with Rome without becoming part of the Roman Empire.

Similarly, an imported object at a Gujarat port does not necessarily mean that a merchant travelled directly from its place of manufacture to Gujarat. Goods could pass through several intermediary markets.

Prelims focus

  • Myos Hormos and Berenice were important Red Sea ports of Roman Egypt.
  • Barygaza participated in Arabian Sea trade connecting India with Roman Egypt and West Asia.
  • The south-west monsoon assisted voyages toward India's western coast.
  • The north-east monsoon could assist return voyages toward western markets.
  • Roman coins in India indicate commercial connections, not necessarily Roman rule.
  • Trap: Indo-Roman trade was not confined to direct exchange between Roman citizens and Indian merchants.

[NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, 'Traders, Kings and Pilgrims,' pp. 99–100; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns,' pp. 44–45; Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, sections 1, 14, 36, 49 and 57, W. H. Schoff translation, University of Washington Silk Road text, consulted 19 November 2026; Indian Council of World Affairs, 'Roads, Winds, Spices in the Western Indian Ocean,' keynote address, 6 July 2020, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Seasonal winds supported two-way maritime exchange between India and western markets.

title: Roman and West Asian Trade across the Arabian Sea

body:
Lothal: Maritime exchange in the Harappan period

Lothal, in present-day Gujarat, was an important Harappan settlement situated near the Gulf of Khambhat. It belonged to a much earlier period than the Indo-Roman trade associated with Barygaza.

Lothal was connected with the production and movement of craft goods. Evidence of bead-making activity, stone and shell objects, a storage area, seals and sealings indicates that goods were manufactured, collected and exchanged there.

A large basin at Lothal has commonly been interpreted as a dockyard that may have received boats and facilitated the loading or unloading of cargo. The interpretation should be stated with care: the presence of the basin is established, while its exact function has been discussed.

Harappan communities also maintained long-distance contacts with regions beyond the subcontinent, including areas of West Asia. These connections belong to the Bronze Age and should not be confused with Roman trade more than a millennium later.

Dholavira: An important Harappan centre, but a different category

Dholavira was another major Harappan settlement of Gujarat, situated on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kachchh. It was part of the wider Harappan world and its exchange networks.

For a question asking specifically about a well-known Harappan site associated with a large basin interpreted as a dockyard, Lothal is the appropriate identification. Dholavira should not automatically be described as a Roman-period seaport.

Bet Dwarka: Evidence of early historic maritime contact

Bet Dwarka, near Dwarka on Gujarat's western coast, provides another connection with ancient maritime activity. Marine investigations have reported anchors and pottery fragments, including material resembling Mediterranean amphorae.

Some of these objects have been tentatively dated to approximately the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE. They suggest that Bet Dwarka functioned as an anchorage and participated in wider maritime contacts during the early historic period.

The evidence does not establish a Roman political settlement at Bet Dwarka. It is better understood as indicating possible commercial links within the wider Indian Ocean network.

Comparing the periods

Lothal and Bet Dwarka are both connected with maritime activity, but the evidence belongs to different historical settings. Lothal is primarily associated with Harappan trade; the early historic evidence from Bet Dwarka overlaps broadly with the period in which Barygaza was active in Indo-Roman commerce.

Prelims focus

  • Lothal is a Harappan settlement in Gujarat near the Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Lothal is associated with bead-making, storage facilities and a large basin often interpreted as a dockyard.
  • Dholavira is a major Harappan site on Khadir Bet in Kachchh.
  • Early historic maritime material at Bet Dwarka has been tentatively dated to the 1st century BCE–2nd century CE.
  • Trap: The Harappan maritime activity of Lothal is not the same historical phase as the Indo-Roman trade described for Barygaza.

[NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, 'In the Earliest Cities,' pp. 39–40; NCERT, Class 6, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, 'The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation,' pp. 97–99; A. S. Gaur, Sundaresh and S. Tripati, 'Evidence for Indo-Roman Trade from Bet Dwarka Waters, West Coast of India,' International Journal of Nautical Archaeology, vol. 35, no. 1, 2006, pp. 117–127, abstract.]

pictures.alt: Timeline separates Harappan Lothal from early historic Bet Dwarka and Barygaza, comparing their dates and maritime evidence.
pictures.caption: Harappan and early historic maritime activity belong to different periods.

title: Lothal, Bet Dwarka and Gujarat’s Earlier Maritime Connections

body:
Who participated in ancient trade?

Trade depended on several groups rather than a single type of merchant. Farmers and craftspeople produced goods; local traders collected them; caravan merchants transported them inland; and seafaring merchants arranged their movement between ports.

Ancient Indian sources preserve terms for some of these commercial occupations and associations.

  • Setthi or shreshthin: A wealthy merchant or merchant-financier. Such traders could possess considerable economic influence.
  • Satthavaha: A merchant associated with the leadership of a travelling trading caravan.
  • Shreni: An association or guild of merchants or craftspeople.

The terms do not describe identical roles. A caravan leader organised movement over land, while a guild brought together people connected with trade or craft production.

What did shrenis do?

Shrenis helped organise economic activity. Craft guilds could obtain raw materials, arrange training and production, and distribute finished products. Merchant guilds helped organise trade.

Some shrenis also received deposits from wealthy individuals and used the money in activities that earned returns. Part of the income could support religious institutions. This shows that merchant and craft associations could perform financial and social functions in addition to exchanging goods.

Merchants and rulers

Rulers had reasons to support commercial routes because trade brought goods, activity and potential revenue into their territories. They could offer protection, supervise important markets and collect dues connected with trade.

At Barygaza, the use of experienced local pilots in the ruler's service demonstrates one practical connection between political authority and maritime commerce.

A Gujarat example: Vishnushena's merchant charter

A charter issued by Vishnushena in 592 CE concerns a merchant community at Lohatagrama in Gujarat. It records a body of merchants known as a vaniggrama and sets out recognised commercial arrangements and privileges.

The charter contains 72 provisions or customary rules concerning the merchant community. Its importance lies in showing that organised merchants sought formal recognition and protection for their commercial activities.

A vaniggrama in this context means an organised body of merchants. It should not be understood merely as a village in which merchants happened to live.

Merchant communities in later maritime networks

By the medieval period, Gujarati trading communities, including Hindu Baniyas and Muslim Bohras, participated extensively in commerce with the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, East Africa and regions farther east. They traded commodities such as textiles and spices and obtained valuable goods from overseas markets.

These communities are important for understanding the development of Gujarat's maritime commerce over time. However, descriptions of their well-established medieval activity should not automatically be transferred unchanged to the Barygaza trade of the 1st century CE.

Prelims focus

  • Shrenis were associations of merchants or craftspeople.
  • A satthavaha was associated with merchant caravans.
  • Some shrenis organised production, trade and financial deposits.
  • Vishnushena's charter of 592 CE concerned merchants at Lohatagrama in Gujarat.
  • Vaniggrama referred to an organised merchant community.
  • Trap: The prominent medieval trade of Gujarati Baniyas and Bohras should not be treated as proof of their identical role in 1st-century Barygaza.

[NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns,' p. 94; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns,' pp. 43–44; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts–II, 'Towns, Traders and Craftspersons,' pp. 79–80; Government of India, Indian Customs: Evolution of Multifaceted Partnerships, 2024, p. 23, discussion of the Vishnushena charter.]

pictures.alt: Producers make goods, caravan leaders move them inland, and coastal merchants move them between ports, with distinct roles for merchant bodies and political authority.
pictures.caption: Different commercial groups connected production, inland markets and overseas trade.

title: Merchants, Guilds and Political Support for Trade

body:
Maritime commerce continued after the early historic period

Gujarat's overseas commercial connections did not end with the period described in the Periplus. During the early medieval centuries, different towns and harbours became important as political centres, inland markets and overseas connections changed.

The central distinction is between the early historic prominence of Bharuch or Barygaza and the later rise of other Gujarat ports, especially Khambhat.

Valabhi and the Maitraka period

Valabhi, in Saurashtra, was the capital of the Maitraka rulers, who were prominent approximately from the 5th to the 8th centuries CE. Valabhi also developed as an important urban and commercial centre connected with the maritime activity of the Gujarat coast.

Its commercial significance was associated with merchants, the movement of goods and links between inland Saurashtra and overseas markets. Valabhi therefore belongs to a later historical setting than the Barygaza described in the 1st-century Periplus.

Sanjan: A trading centre of southern Gujarat

Sanjan is situated in the Umargam area of present-day Valsad district, Gujarat. It developed as a port and commercial settlement with contacts extending across the Indian Ocean.

Evidence from the site places significant activity approximately between the 8th and 14th centuries CE, with particular prosperity during the 10th–12th centuries CE. Material from West Asia and China supports its participation in distant trading connections.

Sanjan is also associated with the history of the Parsi community. For the study of maritime trade, its principal importance is its role as a southern Gujarat port connected with wider commercial networks.

Ghogha and other ports of the Gulf of Khambhat

Ghogha lies on the western side of the Gulf of Khambhat, in the Saurashtra region. Maritime finds associated with the site indicate active Indo-Arabian trading connections, particularly during the 10th–14th centuries CE.

Ports such as Ghogha, Somnath and Diu participated in commercial networks connecting Gujarat's coast with larger maritime markets. Their roles could include receiving ships, handling local cargo and moving goods onward to larger trading centres.

The later rise of Khambhat or Cambay

Khambhat, also called Cambay or Stambhatirtha, emerged as one of the leading ports of Gujarat during the later part of the 1st millennium CE and became especially prominent in the centuries that followed.

Its commercial importance was strengthened by access to productive inland regions and connections with the Arabian Sea. By the 11th–12th centuries CE, Khambhat occupied a major position in the trading networks of western India.

Bharuch and Khambhat are distinct

Bharuch or Barygaza was the major Gujarat port described in the 1st-century CE Periplus. Khambhat or Cambay became especially prominent in the early medieval and medieval periods. Both were connected with the Gulf of Khambhat, but they were separate towns.

Distinguishing Gujarat ports from ports elsewhere in India

Questions about ancient western-coast trade may include names from regions outside present-day Gujarat.

  • Barbaricum: An ancient port associated with the Indus delta, in the region of present-day Sindh.
  • Suppara or Sopara: An ancient western-coast trading centre in present-day Maharashtra.
  • Calliena or Kalyan: Another trading centre in present-day Maharashtra.
  • Muziris: A major ancient port associated with the Malabar coast of present-day Kerala, particularly important for pepper trade.

These ports were connected through broader commercial networks, but they should not be classified as ports of ancient Gujarat.

The chronological distinction involving Surat

Surat became a major gateway for trade with West Asia during the Mughal period, especially in the early modern centuries. Its later commercial importance does not make it the same port as ancient Barygaza.

One-glance revision of the entire subtopic

The history of Gujarat's maritime commerce is best remembered as a sequence of changing trading centres. Harappan Lothal demonstrates much earlier coastal exchange; early historic Barygaza illustrates inland and Roman-West Asian connections; and Valabhi, Sanjan, Ghogha and Khambhat illustrate the development of later maritime networks.

Prelims focus

  • Valabhi was the capital of the Maitrakas and an important commercial centre.
  • Sanjan, in present-day Valsad district, participated in Indian Ocean trade during the early medieval and medieval centuries.
  • Ghogha was associated with Indo-Arabian trade in the Gulf of Khambhat.
  • Khambhat is also called Cambay or Stambhatirtha.
  • Barbaricum, Sopara, Kalyan and Muziris were not ports of present-day Gujarat.
  • Trap: The prominence of Khambhat and Surat belongs mainly to later periods than the classical Barygaza described in the Periplus.

[Annette Schmiedchen, 'Maitrakas,' Encyclopedia of Ancient History: Asia and Africa, 2021, abstract; Kurush F. Dalal, 'In Pursuit of the Parsis: The Discovery and Excavations at the Early Medieval Entrepôt of Sanjan,' Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts lecture abstract, 2016, p. 1; A. S. Gaur, 'Ghogha: An Indo-Arabian Trading Post in the Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay), India,' International Journal of Nautical Archaeology, vol. 39, no. 1, 2010, pp. 146–155, abstract; Ranabir Chakravarti, 'The Commercial Network of Gujarat in the Light of the Jewish Documentary Geniza (Eleventh–Twelfth Centuries),' in Transregional Trade and Traders, Oxford University Press, 2019, pp. 123–140, abstract; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts–II, 'Towns, Traders and Craftspersons,' p. 84; Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, sections 38–39 and 52–56, W. H. Schoff translation, University of Washington Silk Road text, consulted 19 November 2026.]
